title: A Simple Way to Advocate for Yourself and Your Team: The STAR Technique
author: Carey Nieuwhof
summary: The Good Boss presents the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) framework for translating work into compelling advocacy narratives. Strong work often goes undervalued not from lack of substance but lack of advocacy; good intentions fail in moments when team members are absent. STAR moves from vague praise ('He stepped up') to concrete evidence by setting context, clarifying stakes, specifying actionable steps, and quantifying outcomes. The framework works because it moves from opinion to evidence—people can challenge opinions but struggle to challenge data. Applied to team advocacy, performance reviews, or personal readiness for advancement, STAR provides structure for making compelling cases grounded in specifics rather than personality.
points: Strong work gets undervalued not because it lacks substance but because it lacks clear advocacy; vague praise cannot compete with structured evidence.
The STAR framework—Situation, Task, Action, Result—translates experience into compelling, credible narratives by grounding claims in concrete context and measurable outcomes.
Evidence-based advocacy moves the conversation from 'this person is great' to 'here is what they did, why it mattered, and what changed because of it'—a shift that is harder to challenge.
In moments when team members are absent (calibration meetings, promotion discussions), a leader's ability to advocate determines whether strong work gets recognized and rewarded.
STAR applies equally to personal advocacy for one's own readiness, visibility, or opportunity as it does to advocating for team members.
quotes: There will be moments when you need to make the case for your own readiness, your own impact, or your own growth. Maybe it's a bigger role, or a more challenging assignment, or even a seat at a more strategic table.
You need to translate 'great work done' into an 'impactful story' that people can understand, trust, and remember.
People can challenge your opinions, but it's way harder to challenge hardcore evidence.
One of the responsibilities of a manager is not just to support their team while they do the work. It's also to advocate for them when they're not in the room.
A lot of strong work gets undervalued not because it lacked substance, but because it lacked advocacy.” Archived from The Good Boss on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
